library(tidyverse)

# Rearranging & summarising {background="#1565C0"}

## The `tidyverse` verbs {style="font-size: 0.5em;"}

```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
```

We illustrate with the `penguins` dataset:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
penguins
```

## `select()` columns {style="font-size: 0.5em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
my_penguins <- select(penguins, species, island, sex, bill_length_mm, body_mass_g, year)
my_penguins
```

## `filter()` rows {style="font-size: 0.5em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
filter(my_penguins, sex == "female")
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
filter(my_penguins, sex == "female", island == "Biscoe")
```

## `mutate()` new columns {style="font-size: 0.5em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
mutate(my_penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)
```

. . .

Conditionally, with `replace()`:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
mutate(my_penguins,
       bill_length_mm = replace(bill_length_mm, bill_length_mm > 39, 100))
```

## Pipes `|>` {style="font-size: 0.5em;"}

The pipe passes the result on the left into the next function, so you can chain
verbs into a readable recipe:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: FALSE
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3|4|5|6"
penguins |>
    select(species, island, sex, body_mass_g, bill_length_mm) |>
    mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) |>
    filter(sex == "female") |>
    arrange(bill_length_mm) |>
    select(-body_mass_g)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE
#| eval: TRUE
penguins |>
    select(species, island, sex, body_mass_g, bill_length_mm) |>
    mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) |>
    filter(sex == "female") |>
    arrange(bill_length_mm) |>
    select(-body_mass_g)
```

## Summarise by group {style="font-size: 0.5em;"}

`group_by()` + `summarise()` collapse each group to a single row:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: FALSE
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3"
penguins |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(average_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE
#| eval: TRUE
penguins |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(average_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

## Mutate by group {style="font-size: 0.5em;"}

`group_by()` + `mutate()` keep every row but compute within each group:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
penguins |>
    select(species, island, bill_length_mm) |>
    group_by(species) |>
    mutate(
        species_average = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
        dist_from_average = bill_length_mm - species_average
        )
```

## Joining data frames {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}

- `left_join()`: all rows from x
- `right_join()`: all rows from y
- `full_join()`: all rows from both x and y
- `inner_join()`: only rows with a match in both
- `semi_join()`: rows from x with a match in y, keeping only x's columns
- `anti_join()`: rows from x with **no** match in y

## Example {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
x <- data.frame(
  id = c(1, 2, 3),
  value_x = c("x1", "x2", "x3")
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo=TRUE
x
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
y <- data.frame(
  id = c(1, 2, 4),
  value_y = c("y1", "y2", "y4")
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo=TRUE
y
```
:::
:::

# Pivoting {background="#1565C0"}

```{r}
customers <- read_csv(here::here("assets/class4/customers.csv"))
prices <- read_csv(here::here("assets/class4/prices.csv"))
```

## Case study {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo=TRUE
customers
```

:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

```{r}
#| echo=TRUE
prices
```
:::
:::

## Desired output {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

```{r}
#| echo=FALSE
customers |>
  pivot_longer(cols = item_1:item_3, names_to = "item_id", values_to = "item") |>
  left_join(prices)
```

## From wide to long: `pivot_longer()` {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
customers
```

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
#| code-line-numbers: "2,6|3|4|5"
purchases <- customers |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(item_1, item_2, item_3),  # columns to pivot
    names_to = "item_id",              # names -> new column item_id
    values_to = "item"                 # values -> new column item
    )
purchases
```
:::
:::

## From long to wide: `pivot_wider()` {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Going back from purchases to customers:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2,5|3|4"
purchases |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = "item_id",   # column names
    values_from = "item"      # values in columns
    )
```

## Putting it together {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
purchases |>
  left_join(prices)
```

# Import {background="#1565C0"}

## Work inside an R Project {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}

Before reading any data, organise your work in an **RStudio Project**: a folder
that contains your scripts *and* your data.

- `File -> New Project ...` in RStudio creates the project folder.
- Move your data file (e.g. `employees.xlsx`) inside that folder.

. . .

The `here` package builds file paths **relative to the project root**, so you
never hard-code absolute paths like `C:/Users/...` and never need `setwd()`. The
same code then runs on any machine or collaborator's laptop:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: FALSE
library(here)

i_am("practice1.R")               # declare where this script lives
path <- here("data", "employees.xlsx")  # build the path to the data
path
```

- `i_am()` tells `here` which file you're running, so it can locate the root.
- `here("data", "employees.xlsx")` then always points to `<project>/data/employees.xlsx`.



## Reading Excel files: `read_xlsx()` {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}

Proprietary spreadsheets (`.xls`, `.xlsx`) need the `readxl` package:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: FALSE
library(readxl)

path <- here("data", "employees.xlsx")
dt <- read_xlsx(path = path)
```

. . .

An Excel file can contain **several sheets**. Pick one with the `sheet` argument:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: FALSE
purchases <- read_xlsx(path = path, sheet = "purchases_history")
products  <- read_xlsx(path = path, sheet = "products")
```

## Save your results {style="font-size: 0.5em;"}

Use `here()` to write files into your project too. Take a result like:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
my_res <- penguins |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(average_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
my_res
```

**As an R data object:**

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: FALSE
save(my_res, file = here("my_results.rda"))  # save
load(here("my_results.rda"))                 # load next time
```

**As an Excel file:**

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: FALSE
library(writexl)
write_xlsx(my_res, path = here("my_results.xlsx"))
```

# Cleaning {background="#1565C0"}

## Inconsistent column names {style="font-size: 0.55em;"}

Real files rarely have tidy names: spaces, random capitalisation, dots...

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
raw <- data.frame(`Last NAME` = c("Curie", "Franklin"),
                  `First-name` = c("Marie", "Rosalind"),
                  `Seniority` = c(12, 7),
                  check.names = FALSE)  # keep the messy names as-is
raw
```

. . .

`clean_names()` from the `janitor` package standardises them to `snake_case`:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
library(janitor)
clean_names(raw)
```

## Missing values {style="font-size: 0.55em;"}

Missing entries are stored as `NA`. `summary()` reports them column by column:

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE
#| eval: TRUE
my_df <- data.frame(
    id = 1:5,
    ad_type = c("pop-up", "banner", "video", "banner", "pop-up"),
    n_clicks = c(56, 23, 321, NA, 10),
    sales = c(7, NA, 25, 10, 23))
```

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
my_df
```

. . .

**Locate** them with `is.na()`:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
is.na(my_df$n_clicks)
```

## Missing values: imputation {style="font-size: 0.55em;"}

A common fix is to **replace** missing values with a summary of the column, e.g.
its median. With the tidyverse, combine `mutate()` and `replace()`:

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| eval: TRUE
my_df |>
  mutate(n_clicks = replace(n_clicks, is.na(n_clicks),
                            median(n_clicks, na.rm = TRUE)))
```

. . .

Remember: any operation involving `NA` returns `NA`, so always pass
`na.rm = TRUE` to the summary function.
